heading: What Type of Queries You Write or What Are the Tables Used in Your Project
content:
Usually, I get a request through Jira to generate a report --- they
create a sub-task for it. We have quite a few tables in our project,
around 70 of them.

Just as an example, assuming the project is called SPG --- we've got
tables like

- spg_newcustomer, which holds customer details,

- spg_supplier_details for payment details,

- spg_salesperson for sales person info,

- spg_invoice_details for invoice details,

- spg_order for order details, and

- spg_order_details

which has all the order details including the actual items ordered.

Most of the time, the sub-tasks I get are things like --- total number
of sales made by a salesman in a day, week, month, or quarter, number of
orders pending in a day or week, number of failed orders, number of
users who opted for returns and refunds, or sales volume for a
particular product or category on a given day.

I write a SQL query, extract the data as an Excel file, and send it over
to the user.

heading: What Does Your Application Do
content:
So, I worked on the First Heritage Bank Online Banking Application ---
that's the primary digital banking platform for the bank's retail and
small business customers.

It's built on a microservices architecture using Spring Boot and REST
APIs, deployed on Apache Tomcat servers on Linux, with an Oracle
database as the backend.

The application has quite a few major modules --- Login and Dashboard,
Accounts, Payments, Loans, Cards, Statements, and an Operations console.

Starting with Login and Dashboard that's the entry point for every
customer. It handles secure authentication using MFA, so things like
OTP, security questions, or biometric login on mobile.

Once they log in, the dashboard gives them a full 360-degree view of
their finances --- checking, savings, CDs, IRAs, 401ks, mortgages,
HELOCs --- all in one place, along with recent transactions, pending
payments, and alerts.

Accounts module lets customers view and manage all their deposit and
lending accounts in real time --- checking, savings, money market, CDs,
IRAs, all of that.

Payments was probably the busiest and most critical module --- it
supports multiple rails: ACH for domestic transfers and payroll, wire
transfers both domestic and international, Zelle for instant P2P
payments, and Bill Pay utilities etc.

Loans module covers mortgages, HELOCs, auto loans, personal loans,
student loans.

Cards handles credit, debit, and ATM cards --- customers can
activate or deactivate cards, set travel notices, dispute transactions,
manage PINs and limits, or replace a lost card.

Finally, Statements --- that module generates and delivers monthly,
quarterly, and ad-hoc statements across all account types, with support
for e-statements and PDF downloads.

So overall, this is my banking platform, and my role was mainly around
production support --- keeping these modules running smoothly,
monitoring for issues, and resolving them quickly within SLA.

heading: How do you monitor application activity in production? Walk me through your approach.
content:
For real-time monitoring, I prefer a dual approach. If I'm already on
the server, I use sudo journalctl -u fhb-app -f --- it tails the system
service logs instantly. As I interact with the UI, I see the exact
requests and responses flowing through.

I use AWS CloudWatch: navigate to Log Groups → fhb-app-logs → the
fhb-app-server stream → Start Tailing.

It gives the same live view without needing SSH or PuTTY, which is much
better in a meeting.

This setup helped us quickly correlate UI actions with backend behaviour
during troubleshooting."

heading: Walk me through how you would investigate why a customer cannot log in.
content:
I'd start in the database. For Daniel Williams (FHB-10032), his customer
record shows IS_ACTIVE = 0, which directly blocks login.

I'd then run the full set of related queries to check accounts, any
pending reactivation requests, support tickets, and audit logs.

In this case, there was a pending reactivation request meant for the Ops
Console --- a maker-checker workflow where an Agent raises the request
and a Reviewer approves it.

This prevents unilateral changes and adds proper controls.

I'd also tail the application logs while attempting login to see any
specific error messages or authentication service calls.

This combination of logs + targeted SQL gives a complete picture very
quickly."

heading: What tables or data points would you look at to get a 360° view of a customer?
content:
I start with the core customer table, then join to accounts (checking,
savings, CDs, etc.), then go deeper into transactions, transfers, cards,
loans, statements (including the S3 key for the PDF), support tickets,
and any change-request audit trail.

For system context, I also reference tables like FHB_ACH_BATCH for
overnight processing and FHB_OPS_USER for internal staff handling
requests.

I even wrote a bonus query that shows two customers side-by-side with
counts of accounts, cards, loans, tickets, and pending requests ---
super useful for quick comparisons during reviews.
